newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian president holds on to power in marred poll.
newsitem.headline: Zambian president holds on to power in marred poll.

text.p: Zambian election results showed on Tuesday that President Frederick Chiluba would win a second term, having barred his only serious rival in what diplomats called a ruse that appeared to have worked.
Chiluba won up to 90 percent of a third of votes counted so far in the direct presidential poll.
It went ahead without "Father of the Nation" and former president Kenneth Kaunda, who called for economic sanctions on Zambia to punish what he called a rigged election.
Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) won 39 of 42 constituencies declared in the 150-seat parliament of a poor country that is riddled with debt despite rich copper reserves.
Final results were awaited by Wednesday but observers said nothing could stop Chiluba, 53, winning.
Supporters wearing Chiluba's effigy on tee-shirts danced in celebration on pickup trucks that circled the capital Lusaka, but more political strife for Zambia loomed.
Dean Mung'omba, one of his four minor rivals who took part in the poll, told reporters there had been "massive rigging and electoral fraud" and his party would not recognise the new government.
"Having pursued all peaceful options and civilised methods of political conduct, (my) Zambian Democratic Congress now reserves the right to pursue other alternatives," he said.
Kaunda, who ruled Zambia from independence in 1964 until Chiluba trounced him in 1991's first free polls, was barred by a new law because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian.
The law enraged the MMD's opponents and foreign observers.
Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) boycotted what it called a farce to protest at his exclusion and on Tuesday Kaunda urged sanctions to force a fresh vote.

"I am looking for the time when the foreign donor community will be supported by the governments in SADC (the Southern African Development Community) and impose sanctions on us," the 72-year-old veteran statesman told Reuters in an interview.
A spokesman for Chiluba laughed off the suggestion.

Donor nations have frozen vital aid to Zambia this year, hoping to repeal the bar on Kaunda and stop intimidation of the press. But they conceded that they may have to cave in after Chiluba ignored pressure from them, his domestic opponents and South African President Nelson Mandela.
"Sooner or later the freeze will ease up, but probably not before the end of the year," one Western diplomat said.
"We have shown our short-term reaction to their short-term actions but we also have to think in the longer term."

An indefinite halt to balance-of-payments support, that donors give to help Zambia cope with a vast $6.4 billion debt, would cripple a country which is still a World Bank model of African economic reform despite its political setbacks.
Chiluba blames the economic mess on socialist-oriented mismanagement during Kaunda's one-party state. Many Zambians, who gave the MMD 125 seats in 1991, agree.
Political analysts say Chiluba would have beaten Kaunda this time round anyway, but seemed too scared to risk it.

If outside pressure crumbles rather than growing as Kaunda wants, he could be nearing the end of a political career that helped end colonialism across southern Africa, and his party could fade away, anaylsts and diplomats said.
"If you are not in parliament and have five years ahead of you -- I can't see them surviving politically, and Kaunda is not getting any younger," one diplomat said.
